contexts.park_guell:
Park Güell (part of Park Güell). Materials: local stone (viaducts and columns), trencadís (broken tile/ceramic mosaic). Inspired by the English garden-city movement (hence the English word 'Park' in its name); marks Gaudí's 'naturalist period', in which his study of nature and organic forms drove both ornament and underlying structural geometry. Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel). Uses inverted catenary arches for its viaducts and elevated pathways, the same load-bearing-compression method Gaudí used earlier at Colònia Güell. Entry to the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, gate area) has required a paid ticket since October 2013; Barcelona residents enter free. UNESCO's 1984 inscription describes the park's architecture as combining the Arts and Crafts movement, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism, and as having presaged techniques of 20th-century Modernism. Introduced curved, undulating benches at Park Güell -- a precursor to the style Gaudí later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as Casa Milà.
---
Related: Catenary/compression structural logic shared with the Espai Gaudí attic at Casa Milà, though executed in stone viaducts here versus brick vaulting there.
contexts.drac_park_guell:
The Dragon / Salamander (El Drac) (part of park_guell). Materials: trencadís (tile-shard mosaic), masonry/mortar core. Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery, though sources disagree on whether the figure represents a dragon or a salamander -- the official park site itself uses both terms. Functions as the overflow spout of the park's rainwater system: water falling on the Greek Theatre/Nature Square above is collected by a conduit inside the Hypostyle Room's colonnade and channeled to an underground cistern, with the dragon's mouth as that system's overflow outlet. Covered in trencadís (tile-shard mosaic); the official park site calls it 'the most popular image of the park.' Sits on the Dragon Stairway, a twin flight of steps divided into three landings: goblin-like shapes on the first landing, the emblem of Catalonia on the second, and the dragon/salamander further up.

contexts.porxada_bugaderia:
Laundry Room Portico (Pòrtic de la Bugaderia) (part of park_guell). Materials: unworked (rough-cut) hillside stone. Described by the park's own site as taking 'the shape of a great wave atop slanting columns' -- called one of the finest examples of Gaudí's organic architecture; the slanted double colonnade evokes a stone forest, echoing how the park's viaduct columns and vaults elsewhere mimic tree trunks and natural forms. The double colonnade of slanting columns acts as a structural buttress against the retaining wall behind it -- the tilt is load-bearing, not decorative. Uses the same structural logic as the park's viaducts: inclined stone columns form a parabola/inverted-catenary profile so the columns work in pure compression along the line of thrust, without needing external buttressing.

Whimsical, fairy-tale-like pavilion forms marking the park's main entrance, reflecting Güell's ambition to recreate an English residential-park model. One of the two pavilions originally housed a phone booth; the other now contains a permanent exhibit of the Barcelona City History Museum. Forms a pair of gatehouses flanking the park's main entrance, among the first structures built on site.

contexts.banc_serpentejant:
Serpentine Bench (Banc Serpentejant) (part of park_guell). Materials: trencadís (broken tile/ceramic/glass mosaic). Its ergonomic, curving form creates enclaves along its length that encourage social interaction rather than facing visitors outward in a straight line. Sits directly atop the Hypostyle Room's vaulted terrace, following the ergonomic curve designed to double as a shared social space rather than a simple boundary wall. One of Gaudí's introductions of curved, undulating bench forms at Park Güell, a precursor to the style he later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.

Functions as part of the park's rainwater collection system: a conduit inside the colonnade gathers water falling on the terrace above and channels it to an underground cistern, ultimately overflowing through the dragon's mouth. Ceiling mosaics recall grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.

contexts.viaductes_park_guell:
Viaducts / elevated pathways (part of park_guell). Materials: local stone. Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, blending the paths seamlessly with the surrounding landscape. As with Gaudí's earlier work at Colònia Güell, the viaducts use inverted catenary arches to achieve optimal load-bearing compression, so the stone columns work in pure compression without needing external buttressing. Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, part of Gaudí's naturalist-period design language for the park.

contexts.la_pedrera:
Casa Milà (La Pedrera) (part of Casa Milà (La Pedrera)). Materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, lower floor; Villefranche quarry, upper floors), wrought iron, curved iron floor beams. Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa. Self-supporting stone facade with no load-bearing walls, connected to curved iron beams surrounding the perimeter of each floor -- allowing interior walls to be added or removed without affecting the building's stability. In August 1908 the City Council fined the project for exceeding its permitted height and site boundaries; the dispute was resolved in December 1909 when the building was certified as monumental and exempted from strict bylaw compliance. Nicknamed 'La Pedrera' ('the stone quarry') by residents who disliked its rough-hewn, undulating stone facade -- an insult that became its popular name. Considered a predecessor of later biomorphic buildings such as the 1921 Einstein Tower (Erich Mendelsohn), the Guggenheim Museum (Frank Wright), and Frank Gehry's Disney Concert Hall.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as Park Güell.

contexts.catenaria_pedrera:
Espai Gaudí attic (catenary/parabolic brick arches) (part of la_pedrera). Materials: brick (volta catalana / timbrel vaulting). The rippling roofline is widely compared to the ribs of a huge animal or the fronds of a palm; the space, now called Espai Gaudí, is often described as feeling like walking through the inside of a whale's ribcage. Built using volta catalana (Catalan/timbrel vault) technique -- thin layered brick vaulting imported from Italy in the 14th century, laid without a full wooden centering framework. Arch height and spacing directly follow the courtyards' footprint below: arches rise higher where the plan narrows and drop lower where it widens, so the roof structure encloses the irregular figure-8 courtyard shape beneath it. 270 parabolic brick arches of varying height, spaced about 80 cm apart, give the roofline a rippling, organic silhouette.

contexts.caps_pedrera:
Chimneys and rooftop sculptures ('caps') (part of la_pedrera). Materials: brick, lime coating, broken marble, broken Valencia tiles, glass (one chimney). Nicknamed the 'garden of warriors' by poet Pere Gimferrer, since the grouped chimneys look like helmeted sentinels standing guard over the skylight/staircase exits; their helmet-like silhouettes are sometimes linked to Gaudí's interest in medieval fortress architecture. The roof holds 28 chimneys in several groupings, 6 skylight/staircase exits, 2 half-hidden vents that renew air inside the building, and 4 discharge domes -- all functional rather than purely decorative. Some staircase-exit towers double as housings for the building's water tanks, a few of which are snail-shaped. The rooftop underwent a later restoration that removed chimneys added after Gaudí's death, TV antennas, and other additions, to return the roofscape closer to its originally designed functional layout. One chimney is topped with glass -- reportedly added by Gaudí the day after the building's inauguration party using empty champagne bottles, later restored with early-20th-century champagne-bottle bases.
---

contexts.facana_pedrera:
Self-supporting stone facade (part of la_pedrera). Materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, first floor), limestone (Villefranche quarry, higher levels), wrought iron (balconies). Viewed from outside, the building reads in three parts: the main six-storey block with winding stone floors, two set-back floors with a smoother, whiter, wave-like curve, and the body of the roof. Self-supporting: free of load-bearing walls, with the facade connected to curved iron beams around the perimeter of each floor, allowing large window openings and free interior layouts. Original lower-level wrought ironwork was removed in 1928 when a tailor's shop opened in the building; one surviving balcony grille was later donated to MoMA, where it is on display. The undulating, rough-hewn stone facade and twisting wrought-iron balconies were controversial when built, giving rise to the 'La Pedrera' (stone quarry) nickname.
---

contexts.patis_pedrera:
Courtyards and interior gate (part of la_pedrera). Materials: cast iron (pillars, beams), wrought iron (gate). The floor-support beam structure was interpreted by Josep Maria Carandell, who built the centerpiece at a shipyard, as representing the helm of a ship -- 'the soul of the building,' with a resemblance to Gothic crypts. The iron entrance gate's non-symmetrical structure evokes soap bubbles formed between the hands, or the structure of a plant cell. The courtyard floor's central support girder combines two concentric cylindrical beams with stretched radial beams, functioning as a keystone working in both tension and compression -- structurally described as 'the soul of the building.' The interior iron gate originally served both pedestrians and cars, providing access to the basement garage (now an auditorium). The two entrance halls are fully polychrome, with oil paintings on the plaster surfaces referencing mythology and flowers.

contexts.sagrada_familia:
Sagrada Família (part of Sagrada Família). Materials: Montjuïc stone (early phases), stone from the Withnell quarry, England (from 2018), post-tensioned stone (later construction phases), Venetian glass mosaic (pinnacles). Conceived as an 'expiatory temple' funded only by private donations, inspired by the basilica of Loreto after Bocabella's 1872 trip to the Vatican; it combines Gothic forms with Gaudí's own curvilinear Art Nouveau. The interior columns are a design unique to Gaudí: their cross-section passes from square to octagonal, then sixteen-sided and finally circular, through the intersection of helicoidal columns. The Passion facade contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), in which the rows and columns add up to 33. The Tower of Jesus Christ was deliberately designed one metre lower than the hill of Montjuïc, because Gaudí believed his work should not surpass God's. The temple has three great facades: the Nativity (the most ornate, finished before 1936), the Passion (austere and hard-lined, sculpted by Josep Maria Subirachs) and the Glory (the largest, still incomplete). The spires represent, in ascending order of height, the Twelve Apostles, the four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and, tallest of all, Jesus Christ.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and Casa Batlló; only partly covered (the crypt and the Nativity facade) by the 2005 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' inscription -- unlike Park Güell and Casa Milà, which were listed in full in 1984.
contexts.cupula_sagrada_familia:
Crossing Vaults and the Tower of Jesus Christ (part of sagrada_familia). Materials: post-tensioned stone. Gaudí wanted a visitor standing at the main entrance to see the nave, crossing and apse vaults rising in ascending perspective. Hyperboloid forms become more pronounced in Gaudí's later design work, particularly from 1914 onwards. At 172.5 m, the Tower of Jesus Christ made the Sagrada Família the tallest church in the world, 11 m above the previous record holder, Ulm Minster.

contexts.facana_naixement:
Nativity Facade (part of sagrada_familia). Materials: hand-carved stone. Dedicated to the birth of Jesus; it faces north-east, towards the rising sun, as a symbol of Christ's birth. Gaudí chose to build it first because he considered it the most attractive and approachable for the public. At the foot of each of the great pillars separating the porticos sits a tortoise (one land, one sea), a symbol of unchanging time; two chameleons at the sides symbolise change. The Tree of Life rises above the door of Jesus, in the portico of Charity. Sagrada Família (part of Sagrada Família). Materials: Montjuïc stone (early phases), stone from the Withnell quarry, England (from 2018), post-tensioned stone (later construction phases), Venetian glass mosaic (pinnacles). Conceived as an 'expiatory temple' funded only by private donations, inspired by the basilica of Loreto after Bocabella's 1872 trip to the Vatican; it combines Gothic forms with Gaudí's own curvilinear Art Nouveau. The interior columns are a design unique to Gaudí: their cross-section passes from square to octagonal, then sixteen-sided and finally circular, through the intersection of helicoidal columns. The Passion facade contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), in which the rows and columns add up to 33. The Tower of Jesus Christ was deliberately designed one metre lower than the hill of Montjuïc, because Gaudí believed his work should not surpass God's. The temple has three great facades: the Nativity (the most ornate, finished before 1936), the Passion (austere and hard-lined, sculpted by Josep Maria Subirachs) and the Glory (the largest, still incomplete). The spires represent, in ascending order of height, the Twelve Apostles, the four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and, tallest of all, Jesus Christ.

Related: A deliberate contrast with the Passion facade: Gaudí explained that starting with a facade as hard and bony as the Passion would have driven the public away.

Dedicated to the Passion and death of Christ, facing west (the setting sun, a symbol of Christ's death); Gaudí wanted it to frighten those who looked at it, with 'broken' arches, 'cut' columns and strong chiaroscuro. It contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), altered so that the rows and columns add up to 33 instead of 34. Each of the four spires is dedicated to an apostle (James, Thomas, Philip and Bartholomew).

contexts.casa_batllo:
Casa Batlló (part of Casa Batlló). Materials: Montjuïc sandstone, trencadís (ceramic mosaic), coloured glass discs, polychrome ceramic (330 pieces), wrought iron. Commissioned at the height of the rivalry between the bourgeois families of Passeig de Gràcia (the 'Illa de la Discòrdia', the Block of Discord): the textile industrialist Josep Batlló wanted a house that would put the neighbouring buildings by Puig i Cadafalch and Domènech i Montaner in their place. The attic has sixty catenary arches, creating a space that evokes the ribcage of an animal. The central light well is clad in tiles in graded shades of blue (deeper at the top, lighter at the bottom) to spread light evenly between floors. Its popular name 'Casa dels Ossos' (House of Bones) comes from its biomorphic, skeletal look. The arched roofline evokes the back of a dragon or dinosaur; a common reading casts the cross-topped tower as the lance of Saint George driven into the beast's back.

contexts.pla_frontal_casa_batllo:
Main Facade (part of casa_batllo). Materials: Montjuïc sandstone (ground floor and first-floor galleries), coloured glass discs, 330 polychrome ceramic pieces, wrought iron (balconies). The central section evokes the surface of a lake with water lilies, recalling Monet's Water Lilies, through the rippling effect of the glass and ceramic mosaic. The upper crown carries a frieze of ceramic pieces open to various readings; Gaudí reused trencadís fragments left over from other works. The metallic-finish roof tiles mimic the scales of a monster, shading from green (where the head begins) to blue and violet in the centre, and to red and pink at the far left. The tower is topped by a four-armed cross facing the cardinal points and carries the monograms of Jesus (JHS), Mary (M with a ducal crown) and Joseph (JHP) in gilded ceramic. A small triangular window in the roof stands for the dragon's eye.

answers.question: What is special about these lower floors?
answers.answer: The ground floor of Casa Batlló is notable for its unusual tracery, irregular oval windows, and stone carved into sinuous shapes, which are reminiscent of natural forms.
